decision.title: Slices without copies: sequence slices, positional filters, matched bases (packet )
decision.summary: A shares its base vector, a slices a stored input, and the memo remembers matched bases, so recursion over the rest of a sequence is linear.

body.p: , after , , , , , , , , . Running SchXslt 1.10.1 to compile the EN 16931 Schematron rules found recursion over the rest of a sequence quadratic: make_span copied the rest into a new vector unless the input was an integer range, $s[position() > 1] tested every position, and a typed parameter (as element()*) matched every item of the rest on each call. SchXslt's schxslt:replace-params walks 780 parameters this way for each of 1,042 attributes.

item.p: Whom it serves: programs that recurse over a sequence (a common XSLT 2.0 and XQuery idiom: head, then the rest), SchXslt first.

Sequence slices (glossary , , ; src/xdm_sequence.c, internal sxml_sequence_make_slice in src/xdm_internal.h): a sequence cell of its own class holding one reference to a vector (its slice base), a first index and a count. It reports SXML_SEQUENCE_REPRESENTATION_VECTOR and uses the vector's item representation, as the descending range shares the range's (): to every reader it is items in an array in a cell, so no public header changes () and no switch over representations in other files. A slice of a slice has the outer slice's base, so a slice never reads through another: count, get_item and iteration are O(1), and nothing nests (). Reference counts keep the base alive while a slice exists; cells are immutable, so shared items never change.

The copy rule: a span of at most 16 items (SXML_SLICE_MAXIMUM_COPIED_ITEM_COUNT), or one under an eighth of its base's count (SXML_SLICE_MINIMUM_BASE_SHARE), is copied into a new vector. A short vector costs about what a slice cell does, and memory held through a slice stays within eight times what it shows. Recursion over the rest of n items copies n/8 + n/64 + ... items in all: linear. Spans of ranges stay ranges (ascending and now descending); a concatenation or lazy input is read item by item into a vector as far as the span reaches, as before (a lazy input's error is raised as before). Takers: fn:tail, fn:subsequence, fn:trunk, fn:slice with step 1, fn:insert-before; fn:head and fn:foot read one item as before.

Positional filters (glossary ; the evaluator's FILTER, src/evaluator.c; no IR pass is needed): a FILTER whose predicate is one comparison (eq, lt, le, gt, ge, =, <, <=, >, >=, either operand order) of the context position with an atom the FILTER does not bind (a constant, a variable or a global, bound already) is the slice of its input at those positions when the input is stored (empty, one item, a vector, a slice, a range). The other operand must be () (nothing is selected), one inline integer, or, for a general comparison, an integer range: $s[position() = $n to $m] lowers to a comparison with a slot that the hoist pass of binds outside the predicate. Anything else (a double, an untyped value, a sequence of numbers, ne and !=) and concatenation or lazy inputs take the loop as before; comparing two integers raises nothing, so values and errors are those of the loop (XPath 4.0, 4.4.1, 4.11.1, 4.11.2).

Matched bases (src/evaluator_function.c, in sxml_evaluator_match_sequence_type, so coercion, instance of and treat share it): a vector or slice of 16 items or more is matched against a sequence type by its count alone once its base has matched the item type: the evaluation memo () keeps, per item type, the last base of 16 items or more whose every item matched (as a FILTER by type keeps its last input, ), retained until the evaluation ends. A base not in the memo is matched once against the item type with occurrence "*" (at most eight times the slice, by the copy rule); when one of its items fails, the value itself is matched as before. Without this, a typed parameter kept recursion quadratic (2.55 of the 2.73 s of the tail form below).
Steps (): a slice is one step, the call's or the FILTER's turn; a positional filter no longer charges one step per item, and a memo hit charges no matching. Step counts fall, never rise.

Measured (release, processor seconds, before at 86669bc, after with the change; 100 recursive walks over 780 elements, SchXslt's bench-tail.xsl over s1.sch): $items[position() > 1] 10.23 to 0.11, tail($items) 2.55 to 0.11, subsequence($items, 2) 3.03 to 0.11. tests/bench/recursion-tail.xq (new in run-bench.py, the three forms over a constructed document) 17.6 to 0.65; after, 0.23, 0.45, 0.91 and 1.85 s for 780, 1,560, 3,120 and 6,240 elements: linear. SchXslt's expand stage of EN 16931, unpatched (step bound raised 100 times in a scratch build only): 552 to 458 s, the same output byte for byte; the rest is SchXslt's own per-level re-sort (the packet's measurement: 1 min 39 s once removed). Callgrind: xmark-all 8.737 to 8.737 x 10^9 instructions, recursion 6.704 to 6.714; every other benchmark's output the same. QT4 XP40 (32,785 passed), XQ40 (46,114) and XT40 (12,185), whole, release, case by case: 0 outcomes differ.

Left: slices of concatenations and lazy sequences copy (once: the copy is a vector, so later slices share it); fn:remove($s, 1) and $s[position() != 1] take the loop; the matched-base memo keeps one base per item type, so two sequences of one type recursed over in turn match each time.
